title: Classification Metrics III - Multiclass Precision and Recall
abstract:
With more than two classes there is no single "positive" class, so precision and
recall are computed per class by collapsing the problem to one-vs-rest, and
then averaged. This document works the notes' Dog/Cat/Rabbit example in full —
including how to read the row and column totals — and then covers the part the
notes leave implicit but that decides everything in practice: the three averaging
schemes (macro, micro, weighted), what each one hides, and which to report.

blocks.t: Per-Class First
From the notes
Here precision & recall are calculated per class.
\boxed{ F_1\text{ Score}=\frac{F_{1,\text{Dog}}+F_{1,\text{Cat}}+F_{1,\text{Rabbit}}}{3} }

This is macro averaging — the plain mean over classes. It is the
default the notes present, and \S3 explains when it is the right one and when it
is not.
The Worked Example

blocks.cap:
The notes' matrix, with the diagonal highlighted and the two totals
 marked. Precision reads down a column; recall reads across a row.

blocks.t: The rule for reading the matrix
For class $c$, with rows as actuals and columns as predictions:

TP_c = M_{cc},
 \qquad
 FP_c = \underbrace{\sum_{i\neq c}M_{ic}}_{\text{rest of the COLUMN}},
 \qquad
 FN_c = \underbrace{\sum_{j\neq c}M_{cj}}_{\text{rest of the ROW}} .
Therefore

\text{Precision}_c=\frac{M_{cc}}{\text{column total}},
 \qquad
 \text{Recall}_c=\frac{M_{cc}}{\text{row total}} .

Precision divides by the column total; recall divides by the row total.
That single sentence is all you need to compute any multiclass metric by hand.
Check the axis convention first

The notes draw predicted across the top and actual down the side, as
above. scikit-learn's confusion_matrix uses rows $=$ actual, columns $=$
predicted — the same orientation. But many textbooks and papers transpose it, in
which case precision and recall swap places. Always read the axis labels
before interpreting somebody else's matrix.
Reading the result
More useful than either average is the pattern in the off-diagonal cells:

items:
Cat has high recall (0.88) but mediocre precision (0.66). The
 model rarely misses a cat but frequently calls other animals cats — 5
 dogs and 10 rabbits land in the Cat column. It is over-predicting
 Cat.

Rabbit is the weakest class on both measures (0.58, 0.58), and
 its errors go mostly to Cat.

Dog has the best precision (0.86) — when the model says Dog it
 is usually right — but recall is only 0.62, so it misses many dogs,
 mostly calling them rabbits.

blocks.t:
That diagnosis — which classes get confused with which — is
information no single averaged number contains.
The Three Averaging Schemes
Definitions

$$\textbf{Macro:}\quad &\text{Prec}_{\text{macro}}=\frac1C\sum_{c=1}^{C}\text{Prec}_c && \text{every class counts equally}\\[4pt] \textbf{Micro:}\quad &\text{Prec}_{\text{micro}}=\frac{\sum_c TP_c}{\sum_c\left(TP_c+FP_c\right)} && \text{pool the counts, then compute}\\[4pt] \textbf{Weighted:}\quad &\text{Prec}_{\text{weighted}}=\sum_{c}\frac{n_c}{n}\,\text{Prec}_c && \text{weight each class by its support}$$
A fact worth knowing

In single-label multiclass classification — where every sample has
exactly one true class and receives exactly one prediction — every
misclassification is simultaneously a false positive for one class and a false
negative for another. Therefore $\sum_c FP_c=\sum_c FN_c$, and

\text{Precision}_{\text{micro}}=\text{Recall}_{\text{micro}}
 =F_{1,\text{micro}}=accuracy.

So reporting "micro F1" in this setting is just reporting accuracy under a more
impressive name — with all of accuracy's weaknesses on imbalanced data
(Topic 47).

blocks.cap:
The same predictions summarised three ways. The model performs well on
 the 9{,}500-row common class and badly on the two 100-row rare classes. Macro
 exposes that; micro and weighted are dominated by the common class and hide it.

head: Average
Treats
Report it when
rows: Every class equally, regardless of size
The rare classes matter as much as the common ones — disease subtypes, fraud categories. The notes' default
You care about overall correctness. Equals accuracy in single-label problems
You want a single headline number that reflects the population mix

blocks.t: Macro is sensitive to tiny classes

The flip side of macro's virtue: a class with 8 examples contributes as much to
the average as a class with 8{,}000, so its noisy precision can swing the headline
figure. Always print the per-class table with its support column alongside
the average — a metric computed over a handful of rows is not a measurement.
Multi-label is different

If a sample can belong to several classes at once — tagging an article as both
"sport" and "politics" — then $\sum FP_c\neq\sum FN_c$ and micro precision,
micro recall and accuracy all differ. The averaging choice then matters even more,
and micro-F1 becomes a genuinely distinct and commonly reported metric.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score,
                             f1_score, accuracy_score, classification_report)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

labels = ["Dog", "Cat", "Rabbit"]
M = np.array([[25,  5, 10],      # actual Dog
              [ 0, 30,  4],      # actual Cat
              [ 4, 10, 20]])     # actual Rabbit   (rows=actual, cols=predicted)

# =====================================================================
# 1. PER-CLASS PRECISION AND RECALL, STRAIGHT FROM THE MATRIX
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'class':>8s} {'TP':>4s} {'FP':>4s} {'FN':>4s} "
      f"{'precision':>10s} {'recall':>8s} {'F1':>7s} {'support':>8s}")
prec, rec, f1, sup = [], [], [], []
for i, c in enumerate(labels):
    TP = M[i, i]
    FP = M[:, i].sum() - TP          # rest of the COLUMN
    FN = M[i, :].sum() - TP          # rest of the ROW
    p = TP / (TP + FP)               # divides by the COLUMN total
    r = TP / (TP + FN)               # divides by the ROW total
    prec.append(p); rec.append(r)
    f1.append(2*p*r/(p+r)); sup.append(M[i, :].sum())
    print(f"{c:>8s} {TP:4d} {FP:4d} {FN:4d} {p:10.4f} {r:8.4f} "
          f"{2*p*r/(p+r):7.4f} {M[i,:].sum():8d}")

prec, rec, f1, sup = map(np.array, (prec, rec, f1, sup))

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE NOTES' FORMULAS -- the plain mean over the three classes
# =====================================================================
print(f"\nPrecision = (P_Dog + P_Cat + P_Rabbit) / 3 = {prec.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Recall    = (R_Dog + R_Cat + R_Rabbit) / 3 = {rec.mean():.4f}")
print(f"F1 Score  = (F_Dog + F_Cat + F_Rabbit) / 3 = {f1.mean():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. RECONSTRUCT THE LABELS AND CHECK AGAINST SKLEARN
# =====================================================================
y_true, y_pred = [], []
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        y_true += [labels[i]] * M[i, j]
        y_pred += [labels[j]] * M[i, j]
y_true, y_pred = np.array(y_true), np.array(y_pred)

print("\nsklearn confusion_matrix matches:",
      np.array_equal(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels), M))
print(f"macro precision: {precision_score(y_true, y_pred, average='macro'):.4f}")
print(f"macro recall   : {recall_score(y_true, y_pred, average='macro'):.4f}")
print(f"macro F1       : {f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='macro'):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. MICRO AVERAGING == ACCURACY (in single-label problems)
# =====================================================================
TPs = np.diag(M).sum()
FPs = M.sum() - TPs
FNs = M.sum() - TPs
print(f"\nsum of FP = {FPs}   sum of FN = {FNs}   equal: {FPs == FNs}")
# Every mistake is one class's FP and another's FN, so the two sums MUST match.

print(f"micro precision : {TPs/(TPs+FPs):.4f}")
print(f"micro recall    : {TPs/(TPs+FNs):.4f}")
print(f"accuracy        : {accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"sklearn micro F1: {f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='micro'):.4f}")
# All four are the SAME number. Micro-F1 here is accuracy renamed.

# =====================================================================
# 5. WEIGHTED AVERAGING
# =====================================================================
print(f"\nweighted F1 by hand : {np.average(f1, weights=sup):.4f}")
print(f"sklearn weighted F1 : {f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted'):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. WHERE THE THREE DIVERGE -- severe imbalance
# =====================================================================
Mi = np.array([[9500, 300, 200],    # 10 000 of the common class
               [  40,  50,  10],    #    100 of rare A
               [  30,  10,  60]])   #    100 of rare B
li = ["Common", "RareA", "RareB"]

yt, yp = [], []
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        yt += [li[i]] * Mi[i, j]
        yp += [li[j]] * Mi[i, j]
yt, yp = np.array(yt), np.array(yp)

print(f"\n{'average':>10s} {'precision':>11s} {'recall':>9s} {'F1':>8s}")
for avg in ["macro", "micro", "weighted"]:
    print(f"{avg:>10s} "
          f"{precision_score(yt, yp, average=avg, zero_division=0):11.4f} "
          f"{recall_score(yt, yp, average=avg):9.4f} "
          f"{f1_score(yt, yp, average=avg):8.4f}")
print(f"{'accuracy':>10s} {accuracy_score(yt, yp):11.4f}")
# micro/weighted ~ 0.95 (the common class dominates)
# macro          ~ 0.60 (the rare classes drag it down)
# SAME MODEL. The choice of average is a claim about what you care about.

print("\nper-class detail -- always print this:")
print(classification_report(yt, yp, digits=3))

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE DIAGNOSIS THE AVERAGES DESTROY
# =====================================================================
cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels)
print("\nwhere the errors go:")
for i, c in enumerate(labels):
    row = cm[i].copy(); row[i] = 0
    if row.sum():
        worst = labels[int(np.argmax(row))]
        print(f"  {c:>7s} is most often mistaken for {worst:>7s} "
              f"({row.max()} of {cm[i].sum()} = {row.max()/cm[i].sum():.0%})")
print("\nover/under-prediction:")
for i, c in enumerate(labels):
    print(f"  {c:>7s}: predicted {cm[:,i].sum():3d} times, actually occurs "
          f"{cm[i,:].sum():3d} times  -> "
          f"{'OVER' if cm[:,i].sum() > cm[i,:].sum() else 'under'}-predicted")

# =====================================================================
# 8. ON A REAL MODEL
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 6))
logits = np.c_[2*X[:,0], 1.5*X[:,1] - 0.5, X[:,2] + 0.3]
y = np.array(["Dog","Cat","Rabbit"])[logits.argmax(1)]
keep = rng.random(n) < 0.85
y[~keep] = rng.choice(["Dog","Cat","Rabbit"], (~keep).sum())    # add label noise

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)
m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, multi_class="multinomial").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pred = m.predict(X_te)

print("\nconfusion matrix:")
cm = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred, labels=["Dog","Cat","Rabbit"])
print(f"{'':8s}" + "".join(f"{l:>8s}" for l in ["Dog","Cat","Rabbit"]))
for i, l in enumerate(["Dog","Cat","Rabbit"]):
    print(f"{l:8s}" + "".join(f"{v:8d}" for v in cm[i]))
print("\n", classification_report(y_te, pred, digits=3))
Summary
Everything on one page

In multiclass, precision & recall are calculated per class by
 collapsing to one-vs-rest, then averaged.

For class $c$: $TP_c=M_{cc}$, $FP_c$ is the rest of the column,
 $FN_c$ is the rest of the row. So precision divides by the
 column total and recall divides by the row total.

Macro weights every class equally — use it when rare classes
 matter. Micro pools the counts and, in single-label problems,
 equals accuracy. Weighted averages by support.

Because every mistake is one class's FP and another's FN,
 $\sum FP_c=\sum FN_c$, which is why micro precision $=$ micro recall $=$
 micro F1 $=$ accuracy.

Macro exposes failure on rare classes; micro and weighted hide it. The
 choice of average is a claim about what you care about.

Always print the per-class table with support — and read the
 off-diagonal cells, which tell you which classes are confused with

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How do you compute precision for one class in a multiclass problem?

Collapse to one-vs-rest: $TP$ is the diagonal cell, $FP$ is the rest of that
class's prediction column, $FN$ is the rest of its actual row. Then
precision is the diagonal cell divided by the column total, and recall is it
divided by the row total.
Q. Macro or weighted F1?

Macro when every class matters equally regardless of frequency — disease
subtypes, fraud categories, rare defect types. Weighted when you want a headline
number reflecting the population mix. Macro is the more honest choice on
imbalanced data because it refuses to let the common class hide failure on the
rare ones.
Q. Why does micro-F1 equal accuracy?

In single-label multiclass every misclassification is one class's false positive
and another's false negative, so $\sum FP=\sum FN$. Micro precision and micro
recall therefore share a denominator and are equal, and their harmonic mean is the
same number — which works out to the fraction of correct predictions, i.e. 
accuracy.
Q. Macro F1 is 0.61 but weighted F1 is 0.94. What is going on?

The model is good on the common classes and poor on the rare ones. Weighted
averaging is dominated by the large classes; macro gives the rare ones equal
weight and exposes the failure. Print the per-class report to see which classes
are failing.
Q. Cat has recall 0.88 but precision 0.66. What does that tell you?

The model over-predicts Cat: it rarely misses a real cat, but it also labels many
dogs and rabbits as cats. The fix is to look at which classes are leaking into the
Cat column — that is a feature or class-boundary problem, not a threshold one.
Q. What should you always print alongside the averages?

The per-class table with the support column, and the confusion matrix
itself. A precision computed over twelve rows is noise, and the off-diagonal
pattern — which classes get confused with which — is the actionable
information that averaging destroys.
